questions.statement: Report the sentence: He said, 'I am tired.'
questions.context: A friend tells you what his brother said.

options.text: He said that he was tired.
options.feedback: Correct. Reporting verbs trigger backshift, so 'am' becomes 'was' and the pronoun changes to match the reporter's subject.

options.text: He said that he were tired.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were' does not agree with the singular pronoun 'he'.

options.text: He said that I was tired.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I' would be correct only if the reporter were the speaker of the original words.

options.text: He said that he is tired.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is' keeps the original tense, which is only acceptable with a present-tense reporting verb such as says.

questions.explanation:
Reported speech typically shifts the tense one step back and adjusts pronouns and time expressions to the new context.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She said, 'I will call you later.'
questions.context: A student reports a statement about the future.

options.text: She said that she will call me later.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will' does not shift, and retaining it would require a present-tense reporting verb.

options.text: She said that she would call me later.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will' shifts to 'would' in reported speech, and the pronouns are adjusted to the new speaker and listener.

options.text: She said that she would called me later.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Would called' double-marks the future, which is not correct in reported speech.

options.text: She said that I would call her later.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I would call her' reverses the roles of speaker and listener.

questions.explanation:
Will becomes would in reported speech, and the adjustment of pronouns is just as important as the tense shift.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: He said, 'I don't understand this rule.'
questions.context: A teacher reports a student's remark.

options.text: He said that I don't understand this rule.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I' would only be right if the reporter had spoken those words.

options.text: He said that he doesn't understand that rule.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Doesn't' keeps the present negative, which is only correct with a present reporting verb.

options.text: He said that he didn't understand that rule.
options.feedback: Correct. The auxiliary 'do' shifts to 'did' with the base form, and demonstratives may adjust to match the reporting situation.

options.text: He said that he not understood this rule.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not' cannot stand alone before a past participle; the auxiliary is required.

questions.explanation:
Auxiliaries shift just like main verbs: do becomes did, and the main verb returns to its base form.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the yes/no question: She asked, 'Are you coming tonight?'
questions.context: A reporter quotes a witness.

options.text: She asked whether are I coming that night.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whether' requires subject-auxiliary order, so 'whether are I' is not a correct inversion.

options.text: She asked that I was coming that night.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' introduces a statement, not a question, so the meaning changes to an assertion.

options.text: She asked if I am coming tonight.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Am' and 'tonight' both remain unshifted, which requires a present reporting verb.

options.text: She asked if I was coming that night.
options.feedback: Correct. A yes/no question becomes an if-clause in reported speech, with tense backshift and adjusted time expression.

questions.explanation:
A yes/no question loses its inversion in reported speech and is introduced by if or whether, keeping the subject before the auxiliary.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the wh-question: She asked, 'Where do you live?'
questions.context: A student asks about a location in the original conversation.

options.text: She asked where I lived.
options.feedback: Correct. The wh-word stays in front, the auxiliary and the subject are reordered, and the tense shifts back.

options.text: She asked that where I lived.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' introduces a statement and cannot precede a wh-question.

options.text: She asked where lived I.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Where lived I' does not follow the subject-before-auxiliary order of indirect questions.

options.text: She asked where do I live.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Where do I live' keeps the original question order, which is only acceptable with a present reporting verb.

questions.explanation:
Indirect questions use statement word order, so the subject comes before the auxiliary or verb.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She said, 'I saw him yesterday.'
questions.context: An examiner reports a time expression from the original speech.

options.text: She said that she saw him the day before.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Saw' keeps the past simple, which is sometimes possible but the question sets a shifted reporting context.

options.text: She said that she had seen him the day before.
options.feedback: Correct. Past simple shifts to past perfect and 'yesterday' becomes 'the day before' to match the new time of speaking.

options.text: She said that she has seen him yesterday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has seen' is the present perfect and cannot be combined with 'yesterday'.

options.text: She said that I saw him yesterday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I' would only be correct if the reporter had been the original speaker.

questions.explanation:
Time and place expressions are among the words that change in reported speech when the context of speaking moves.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: He said, 'I hadn't finished the report.'
questions.context: A colleague reports a past negative statement.

options.text: He said that I hadn't finished the report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I' would only be correct if the reporter had spoken those words.

options.text: He said that he hasn't finished the report.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Hasn't' shifts the aspect to the present perfect, which changes the temporal meaning of the report.

options.text: He said that he hadn't finished the report.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Hadn't' already marks a past perfect, and reporting a past event keeps that aspect, so no further shift is needed.

options.text: He said that he had not finished the report yet now.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Yet now' is contradictory, since yet and now cannot refer to the same moment.

questions.explanation:
Backshift moves the tense one step, and a past perfect has no further step available, so it stays as it is.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the version that avoids tense backshift legitimately.
questions.context: A grammarian explains the reporting verb.

options.text: He said that he is too busy to help today.
options.feedback: Wrong. A past reporting verb with a present complement normally signals a quotation rather than an indirect report.

options.text: He says that he was too busy to help today.
options.feedback: Wrong. A present reporting verb with a past tense complement is odd unless the past content is intended to remain in the past.

options.text: He said that he was too busy to help today.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Said' combined with 'was' performs backshift, which is also possible but is not the version being asked for here.

options.text: He says that he is too busy to help today.
options.feedback: Correct. A present reporting verb such as says keeps the original tense and time expression, which is entirely correct.

questions.explanation:
Tense backshift is not obligatory in English, and present reporting verbs legitimately preserve the original tense.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which whether is the more suitable conjunction.
questions.context: A study contrasts the uses of if and whether.

options.text: I don't know whether the results have been published.
options.feedback: Correct. Whether is preferred in formal writing and before an 'or' alternative or after a preposition.

options.text: I don't know the results have been published whether.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whether' cannot be stranded at the end of a clause like that.

options.text: I don't know that whether the results have been published.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' and 'whether' cannot both introduce the same clause.

options.text: I don't know if the results have been published.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'If' is acceptable informally, but the item asks for the more suitable formal conjunction.

questions.explanation:
Whether is more formal and is required in positions where if would create ambiguity, particularly before 'or' and after a preposition.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses direct speech correctly.
questions.context: A report quotes an exact wording.

options.text: She said, 'I can't wait to see the results.
options.feedback: Wrong. The sentence lacks the closing quotation mark, which leaves the direct speech unfinished.

options.text: She said, 'I can't wait to see the results.'
options.feedback: Correct. Direct speech keeps the original words and is marked by a reporting verb followed by a comma and quotation marks.

options.text: She said 'I can't wait to see the results.'
options.feedback: Wrong. Direct speech normally requires a comma after the reporting verb when it follows it in the same sentence.

options.text: She said that I can't wait to see the results.
options.feedback: Wrong. After 'that' the sentence is reported speech and the original pronouns are not normally kept.

questions.explanation:
Direct speech preserves the original wording exactly, so pronouns and tense stay as the speaker produced them.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She said, 'I can help you tomorrow.'
questions.context: An exam tests reporting with modal verbs.

options.text: She said that I could help her the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I could help her' reverses the speaker and listener of the original statement.

options.text: She said that she can help me the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Can' does not shift with the reporting verb 'said'.

options.text: She said that she could help me the next day.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Can' shifts to 'could', the pronouns are adjusted and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

options.text: She said that she could helped me the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Could helped' adds a past participle where the modal already carries the tense.

questions.explanation:
Modal verbs shift too: can becomes could and will becomes would when the reporting verb is in the past.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the time expression should change to match the new context.
questions.context: An editor checks reported speech in a novel.

options.text: He said he would arrive the following day here.
options.feedback: Wrong. Placing 'here' at the end is not a standard English word order.

options.text: He said he will arrive here the following day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will arrive' does not shift with the past reporting verb 'said'.

options.text: He said he would arrive here the next day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Here' still points to the original speaker's location, which is wrong in indirect report.

options.text: He said he would arrive here the following day.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Here' refers to the speaker's location, so in a report made elsewhere it becomes 'there', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the following day'.

questions.explanation:
Words such as here, there, today and tomorrow are anchored to the moment of speaking and therefore change when the report is made elsewhere.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the question: She asked, 'What time does the library close?'
questions.context: A conversation exercise requires an accurate report.

options.text: She asked what time the library closed.
options.feedback: Correct. The wh-question keeps its word and takes statement order with the tense shifted back one step.

options.text: She asked at what time was the library close.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was the library close' lacks the participle and reverses the correct order.

options.text: She asked what time the library closes.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Closes' does not shift after the past reporting verb 'asked'.

options.text: She asked what time did the library close.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did the library close' keeps the question order and the auxiliary, which is only acceptable with a present reporting verb.

questions.explanation:
The reporting verb determines the shift: a past verb shifts the tense, while a present verb would leave it unchanged.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She said, 'I have never seen anything like this before.'
questions.context: A lawyer records a client's exact words.

options.text: She said that she has never seen anything like that before.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has' does not shift with the past reporting verb.

options.text: She said that she had never seen anything like that before.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Have' shifts to 'had', the participle stays, and 'this' becomes 'that' as the reference point changes.

options.text: She said that she had never saw anything like that before.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had never saw' uses a simple past form where the participle is required.

options.text: She said that I had never seen anything like that before.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I' would only be right if the lawyer had spoken those words.

questions.explanation:
Present perfect shifts to past perfect in reported speech, and demonstratives like this and that shift along with it.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She said, 'I had finished the report before you arrived.'
questions.context: An exam tests the reporting of a past perfect.

options.text: She said that she had finish the report before I arrived.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had finish' lacks the past participle after the auxiliary.

options.text: She said that she has finished the report before I arrived.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has finished' shifts the past perfect forward to the present perfect, which changes the meaning.

options.text: She said that she had finished the report before I arrived.
options.feedback: Correct. The past perfect has no further step back, so it stays, and the pronoun 'you' becomes 'I' to match the reporter.

options.text: She said that she had finished the report before I did not arrived.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did not arrived' is not a valid structure and 'before' already makes the sequence clear.

questions.explanation:
Backshift applies one step only, so a past perfect remains a past perfect inside the reported clause.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She asked, 'Would you like to join us?'
questions.context: A class practises reporting an invitation.

options.text: She asked whether would I like to join them.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Whether would I' reverses the word order that indirect questions require.

options.text: She asked that I would like to join them.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' introduces a statement and would change the meaning of the question into an assertion.

options.text: She asked if I would like to join them.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'If' is acceptable informally, but the item asks for the more suitable formal conjunction.

options.text: She asked whether I would like to join them.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Whether' is appropriate for a formal report of a yes/no question, and 'us' becomes 'them' for the reporter's perspective.

questions.explanation:
In reported questions, the subject precedes the auxiliary and the original group 'us' is adjusted to the reporter's side.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the statement that best explains the sentence 'She said that she is arriving tomorrow'.
questions.context: A grammar exercise explains an apparent exception.

options.text: The present tense is justified because the content is still true at the time of reporting, which is a common use with certain verbs.
options.feedback: Correct. Reporting a fact that remains true in the present, as with arrangements, commonly retains the original tense.

options.text: The sentence works only because said can be understood as a present-tense reporting verb.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Said' is unambiguously past, so the tense of the reporting verb is not the explanation.

options.text: The sentence is wrong because arriving is not a permitted form after the present tense.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is arriving' is perfectly grammatical with an arrival scheduled for the near future.

options.text: The sentence is wrong because said always requires backshift in every clause.
options.feedback: Wrong. Backshift is a strong tendency rather than an absolute rule, so said does not require it in every clause.

questions.explanation:
Tense backshift in English is a default rather than an obligation, and exceptions are usually justified by the continued truth of the content.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which report best preserves the meaning of 'He asked me whether I had finished' in a formal register?
questions.context: A translator must decide between faithfulness and naturalness.

options.text: He asked me that I had finished the work.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' introduces a statement and removes the question force of the original sentence.

options.text: He asked me whether I had finished the work.
options.feedback: Correct. Whether suits the formal register and the past perfect is preserved because no further backshift is available.

options.text: He asked me whether I did finish the work.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did finish' replaces the perfect with a simple past, which changes whether the completion was still relevant.

options.text: He asked me if I finish the work.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Finish' shifts the past perfect to the present, which loses the earlier completion.

questions.explanation:
Faithful reporting preserves both the question force and the original aspect, while register guides the choice between whether and if.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Report the sentence: She asked me, 'What did you say to the director?'
questions.context: An exam item tests a complex report with an embedded question.

options.text: She asked me what I said what to the director.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'What I said what' repeats the question word and is not a well-formed clause.

options.text: She asked me what did I say to the director.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did I say' keeps the original question order and does not shift the tense.

options.text: She asked me what I had said to the director.
options.feedback: Correct. The wh-word is retained, statement order is used and the past simple shifts to the past perfect.

options.text: She asked me that what I had said to the director.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That' cannot introduce an embedded wh-question.

questions.explanation:
When the reported question is embedded as an object clause, the wh-word stays at the front and the rest takes statement order.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the pair in which the pronouns are correctly adjusted in both sentences.
questions.context: A linguistics exercise examines pronoun shifts in reported speech.

options.text: She told me that their sister had left. / She asked whether our manager would sign it.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Their' signals a plural referent and does not match a singular sister.

options.text: She told me that her sister had left. / She asked whether your manager would sign it.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Your' is used for the person being addressed, so it is wrong for a manager shared by both speakers.

options.text: She told me that his sister had left. / She asked whether our manager would sign it.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'His' would refer to a male speaker and the second clause is the one correctly adjusted.

options.text: She told me that her sister had left. / She asked whether our manager would sign it.
options.feedback: Correct. 'My' becomes 'her' when the speaker changes and 'our' is retained because it includes the person addressed.

questions.explanation: Pronouns in reported speech depend on who is speaking, which is why the same original phrase can become her, my or our.
